lessons.title: Determinate vs. Indeterminate Growth Habits
lessons.body: Soybean plants grow in two main ways: determinate and indeterminate. Determinate varieties stop growing taller once they start flowering. They put all their energy into filling pods. These are often shorter, bushy plants, maturing in a shorter window. Indeterminate varieties keep growing while they flower and set pods. They get taller, produce more leaves, and can yield more over a longer season. In Africa, most commercial varieties are indeterminate because they adapt to varying rainfall. For example, in Nigeria, the variety 'TGX 1448-2E' is indeterminate and yields about 2.5 tonnes per hectare with good management. Determinate types like 'Doko' are common in shorter-season areas of northern Ghana. The choice affects your planting date and spacing. Indeterminate types need wider spacing (75 cm between rows) to allow air movement and reduce disease. Determinate types can be planted closer (50 cm). Also, indeterminate soybeans are more prone to lodging if you apply too much nitrogen. Since soybean fixes its own nitrogen, avoid nitrogen fertilizer; instead, inoculate seed with rhizobia. For a smallholder, indeterminate varieties are often better because they can recover from early stress like drought. But if your rainy season is short (under 100 days), choose determinate. Always check with your local extension officer for the best growth habit for your area. Knowing this helps you plan harvest and avoid losses.

lessons.title: Maturity Groups and Selection Criteria
lessons.body: Soybean varieties are grouped by how many days they take to mature, called maturity groups (MG). Groups range from 000 (very early, 75-85 days) to X (very late, 160+ days). In Africa, most recommended varieties fall in MG III to MG VII. For example, in Zambia, 'Magoye' is MG IV (110-120 days). In Uganda, 'Maksoy 3N' is MG V (120-130 days). Choosing the right maturity group is critical. If you plant a late variety in a short rainy season, pods won't fill before dry weather. If you plant an early variety in a long season, you lose yield potential. Start by finding your local rainfall pattern: how many days of reliable rain do you get? Then pick a variety that matures 10-15 days before the rains normally end. For a 120-day season, choose MG IV (110 days). For 150 days, MG V or VI. Also consider day length: near the equator, day length is stable, so maturity is mostly driven by temperature. In southern Africa, longer days in summer can delay flowering. Tools like the 'Soybean Maturity Group Map' from IITA help. Ask your seed dealer for the maturity group number. If they don't know, avoid that variety. Also look at yield potential: a good variety yields 2-3 tonnes per hectare with proper spacing and inoculant. But don't chase highest yield if it matures too late. A slightly lower-yielding early variety that finishes before drought is better than a high-yielding late one that fails. Always test a new variety on a small plot before planting your whole farm.

lessons.title: GMO, Non-GMO, and Organic Varieties
lessons.body: Soybean varieties come in three main types: GMO (genetically modified), non-GMO (conventional), and organic. GMO soybeans have genes inserted for traits like herbicide tolerance (e.g., Roundup Ready) or insect resistance. In Africa, GMO soybeans are grown commercially only in South Africa. Most other African countries do not allow GMO soybean planting, though some import GMO soy for animal feed. Non-GMO varieties are bred through traditional crossing. They are the standard in Nigeria, Zambia, Ghana, and Kenya. Organic soybeans are non-GMO and grown without synthetic pesticides or fertilizers. They fetch premium prices in export markets, sometimes 20-30% more. But organic yields are often lower (1-1.5 tonnes per hectare) because weeds and pests are harder to control. For a smallholder, non-GMO is usually best: seed is cheaper, you can save seed (though not recommended for hybrids), and local markets accept it. If you want to sell to organic buyers, you need certification, which costs money and takes 2-3 years. GMO seed is expensive and you cannot save it legally. Also, some countries like Kenya require labeling of GMO foods. Before planting, check your country's biosafety laws. In most of Africa, planting GMO soybean without approval is illegal. So stick to non-GMO unless you have a contract with a buyer who wants GMO and you are in a country where it's legal. For organic, start with a small plot, use compost and manual weeding, and find a certified buyer first. Never mix GMO and non-GMO seed in the same field if you want to sell as non-GMO.

lessons.title: Seed Quality and Certification
lessons.body: Good seed is the foundation of a good soybean crop. Poor seed can cut yields by 50% or more. Quality seed has four key attributes: high germination (at least 85%), genetic purity (true to variety), physical purity (no weed seeds or stones), and freedom from disease. In Africa, always buy certified seed from a registered dealer. Look for the certification tag from your national seed authority, like NASC in Nigeria, SCCI in Zambia, or KEPHIS in Kenya. The tag shows the variety name, lot number, germination percentage, and test date. If a seller cannot show a tag, walk away. You can also do a simple germination test at home: count 100 seeds, plant them in a tray of soil, keep moist, and count how many sprout after 7 days. If less than 85 sprout, don't use that seed for planting. Certified seed costs more (about $1-2 per kg) but is worth it. Saved seed from your previous crop often has lower germination and may carry diseases like soybean mosaic virus. If you must save seed, select from healthy plants, dry it well to 12% moisture, and store in a cool, dry place with ash or neem leaves to deter insects. Never use seed from a field with disease. Also, check seed size: larger seeds have more food reserves and emerge stronger. But don't buy based on size alone. Always ask for the variety name and maturity group. For organic production, look for organic-certified seed, which is harder to find but available from some cooperatives. Remember: cheap seed is expensive in the long run.

lessons.title: Regional Adaptation and Yield Potential
lessons.body: Soybean varieties perform differently across Africa's diverse climates. A variety that yields 3 tonnes per hectare in the highlands of Ethiopia may yield only 1 tonne in the lowlands of Mozambique. Regional adaptation means matching a variety to your local rainfall, temperature, soil, and day length. In West Africa, IITA has released many varieties like 'TGX 1835-10E' (yields 2.5 t/ha, matures in 100 days) for the savannas. In East Africa, 'Maksoy' series from Uganda yields 2-2.5 t/ha in 110-120 days. In southern Africa, 'Magoye' is popular in Zambia and Zimbabwe for its drought tolerance, yielding 1.5-2 t/ha. Yield potential is the maximum yield a variety can achieve under ideal conditions. But your actual yield depends on management: planting date, spacing, weeding, and pest control. For example, planting at 60 cm x 10 cm with 2 seeds per hole gives about 333,000 plants per hectare. That density can produce 2.5 t/ha if you control weeds early. If you plant late or skip weeding, yield drops to 0.5 t/ha. Also, soybean needs phosphorus and potassium. Apply 100 kg/ha of NPK 20-10-10 at planting if your soil is poor. But don't apply nitrogen; soybean fixes its own. Inoculate seed with rhizobia (e.g., Biofix) for best results. Check with your local agricultural research station for the best varieties for your district. They often have trial data. Never assume a variety from another region will work for you. Test it first on a small plot. With good management, even a 1.5 t/ha variety can be profitable.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Variety for Your Farm
lessons.body: Choosing the right soybean variety is a decision that affects your entire season. Start by answering four questions: (1) How long is my rainy season? (2) What is my market? (3) What are my pests and diseases? (4) What seed can I afford? For rainfall, count the reliable rainy days. If you have 100-120 days, choose an early maturity group (MG III or IV) like 'Doko' or 'TGX 1448-2E'. If you have 150+ days, choose MG V or VI like 'Maksoy 3N'. For market, if you sell to a processor for oil or feed, any non-GMO variety works. If you sell to organic exporters, you need organic-certified seed. If you sell to a GMO-accepting buyer in South Africa, you can plant GMO. For pests, if you have high soybean rust, choose resistant varieties like 'TGX 1835-10E'. For nematodes, choose resistant varieties like 'UG 5'. For seed cost, certified seed is best but if money is tight, buy a small amount and multiply it: plant 5 kg on 0.2 ha, harvest 100 kg, and plant that next season. But never save seed from hybrid varieties. Also consider your labor: indeterminate varieties need more spacing and may need staking if they lodge. Determinate types are easier to manage. Finally, talk to other farmers in your area. What did they plant last year? What yielded well? Visit a demonstration plot at your extension office. Try at least two varieties on small plots side by side. Measure yield from each. Then scale up the winner. That is the surest way to choose the right variety for your farm.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between determinate and indeterminate soybean varieties?
options: A) Determinate varieties stop growing when flowering starts; indeterminate varieties keep growing while flowering.
B) Determinate varieties are always GMO; indeterminate are non-GMO.
C) Determinate varieties mature later than indeterminate.
D) Determinate varieties have higher oil content.
quiz.explanation: Determinate varieties stop vegetative growth at flowering, while indeterminate varieties continue growing during flowering.

quiz.q: Which growth habit is better for a short rainy season of 100 days?
quiz.explanation: Determinate varieties mature faster and fit short seasons better.

quiz.q: What spacing is recommended for indeterminate soybean varieties?
quiz.explanation: Indeterminate varieties need wider spacing (75 cm) for air movement and disease reduction.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid applying nitrogen fertilizer to soybeans?
options: B) Soybeans fix their own nitrogen from the air
C) It makes the seed poisonous
quiz.explanation: Soybeans form symbiotic relationships with rhizobia bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen.

quiz.q: What is a maturity group in soybeans?
options: A) A group of varieties with similar days to maturity
B) A group of varieties with the same seed size
C) A group of varieties resistant to the same disease
D) A group of varieties from the same country
quiz.explanation: Maturity groups classify varieties by how many days they take to mature.

quiz.q: If your rainy season lasts 120 days, which maturity group should you choose?
quiz.explanation: Choose a variety that matures 10-15 days before the rains end, so Group IV fits a 120-day season.

quiz.q: Which variety is an example of maturity group IV in Zambia?
quiz.explanation: Magoye is a common MG IV variety in Zambia, maturing in 110-120 days.

quiz.q: What tool can help you find the right maturity group for your area?
options: B) A soybean maturity group map from IITA
quiz.explanation: IITA provides maturity group maps that help match varieties to local climates.

quiz.q: Why is it risky to plant a late-maturing variety in a short season?
options: A) It will grow too tall
B) Pods may not fill before dry weather
C) It will attract more pests
D) It will have lower oil content
quiz.explanation: Late varieties need more time to fill pods, and drought at the end of the season can reduce yield.

quiz.q: What should you do if a seed dealer does not know the maturity group of a variety?
quiz.explanation: Without knowing the maturity group, you cannot match the variety to your season, so it's safer to avoid it.

quiz.q: In which African country are GMO soybeans grown commercially?
quiz.explanation: South Africa is the only African country where GMO soybeans are commercially grown.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of non-GMO soybean varieties for smallholders?
options: A) They are always higher yielding
B) They are cheaper and local markets accept them
D) They are resistant to all pests
quiz.explanation: Non-GMO seed is cheaper, can be saved (though not recommended for hybrids), and is accepted in most local markets.

quiz.q: What is required to sell soybeans as organic?
quiz.explanation: Organic certification is a formal process that verifies organic practices and allows premium pricing.

quiz.q: Why is it illegal to plant GMO soybeans in most African countries?
options: B) Biosafety laws do not allow it
D) They cannot grow in Africa
quiz.explanation: Most African countries have biosafety regulations that restrict GMO planting without approval.

quiz.q: What is the minimum germination percentage for good quality soybean seed?
quiz.explanation: Certified seed should have at least 85% germination to ensure good plant stand.

quiz.q: Which organization certifies seed in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: NASC (National Agricultural Seeds Council) is the seed certification authority in Nigeria.

quiz.q: How can you test seed germination at home?
options: A) Soak seeds in water and see if they float
B) Plant 100 seeds in a tray and count sprouts after 7 days
quiz.explanation: A simple germination test involves planting a known number of seeds and counting how many sprout.

quiz.q: What is a danger of saving soybean seed from your own crop?
options: A) It may have lower germination and carry diseases
B) It will always be GMO
C) It will not grow at all
D) It will be too small
quiz.explanation: Saved seed often has lower quality and can carry seed-borne diseases like soybean mosaic virus.

quiz.q: What moisture level should saved soybean seed be dried to for storage?
quiz.explanation: Seed should be dried to about 12% moisture to prevent mold and maintain viability.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of good quality seed?
options: B) High germination, genetic purity, and freedom from disease
quiz.explanation: Quality seed has high germination, genetic purity, physical purity, and is disease-free.

quiz.q: What does regional adaptation mean for soybean varieties?
options: A) A variety performs the same everywhere
B) A variety is matched to local climate, soil, and day length
C) A variety can grow in any country
D) A variety is adapted only to one farm
quiz.explanation: Regional adaptation means choosing a variety that suits your specific local conditions.

quiz.q: Which variety is known for drought tolerance in southern Africa?
quiz.explanation: Magoye is popular in Zambia and Zimbabwe for its drought tolerance.

quiz.q: What is the recommended plant density for soybean to achieve 2.5 t/ha?
quiz.explanation: Spacing of 60 cm x 10 cm with 2 seeds per hole gives about 333,000 plants per hectare.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is recommended for soybean at planting?
quiz.explanation: Soybean needs phosphorus and potassium; NPK 20-10-10 provides these without excess nitrogen.

quiz.q: Why should you inoculate soybean seed with rhizobia?
quiz.explanation: Rhizobia bacteria form nodules on roots and fix atmospheric nitrogen for the plant.

quiz.q: What is the first step in choosing the right variety for your farm?
options: B) Determine the length of your rainy season
D) Choose the highest yielding variety
quiz.explanation: Knowing your rainy season length helps you select a suitable maturity group.

quiz.q: If you have high soybean rust in your area, what should you look for in a variety?
quiz.explanation: Choosing a rust-resistant variety reduces disease pressure and yield loss.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy for a smallholder with limited money for seed?
options: B) Buy a small amount of certified seed and multiply it
C) Use seed from the market
quiz.explanation: Planting a small plot with certified seed and saving the harvest for next season multiplies seed affordably.

quiz.q: Why should you test a new variety on a small plot before planting your whole farm?
options: A) To see if it yields well in your conditions
B) To use up old seed
quiz.explanation: A small trial helps you evaluate yield and adaptation before risking your entire farm.

quiz.q: What is the best source of local advice on choosing soybean varieties?
options: B) Your local agricultural extension officer or research station
quiz.explanation: Extension officers and research stations have trial data and knowledge of local conditions.
